title: AI-assisted scripting and automation
summary: Use AI to generate, explain, and refine PowerShell for endpoint tasks such as Microsoft Graph queries and Intune remediation scripts, then apply a strict verification workflow so you never run untested AI code in production.
objectives: Use AI to generate and explain PowerShell for endpoint tasks like Graph queries and bulk operations
Write effective prompts that state the goal, environment, modules, constraints, and error handling
Generate Intune remediation script pairs (detection + remediation) with AI as a starting point
Always request -WhatIf, confirmation prompts, and safe defaults for any destructive operation
Verify AI-generated scripts: read every line, check cmdlet and parameter names, and confirm Graph scopes
Apply safe practice: test on a pilot device, keep secrets out of prompts, and version-control and peer-review scripts

quiz.q: What is the single most important rule before running an AI-generated PowerShell script against production?
options: Run it on every device at once to save time
Read every line, understand it, and test it on a pilot device first
Trust it because AI wrote it
Delete the comments to make it shorter
quiz.why: AI can hallucinate cmdlets, misuse parameters, or include destructive logic. You must read and understand every line and test on a single pilot device or group before any broad run.

quiz.q: Which PowerShell SDK does AI commonly target for managing Intune and Entra objects programmatically?
quiz.why: The Microsoft Graph PowerShell SDK is the standard way to query and manage Intune, devices, and Entra ID objects from PowerShell, so AI usually generates Graph SDK code for these tasks.

quiz.q: An AI-generated script includes Remove-MgDeviceManagementManagedDevice with no confirmation. What should you add?
options: -WhatIf and/or a confirmation prompt before testing on one pilot device
A second copy of the line
quiz.why: Destructive cmdlets must be run with -WhatIf first and guarded by confirmation, then validated on a single pilot device, so you never bulk-delete by accident.

quiz.q: Why must you check the Microsoft Graph permission scopes an AI-generated script requests?
options: Scopes determine what the script is allowed to do; over-broad or wrong scopes are a security and reliability risk
quiz.why: Graph scopes control authorization. The script may request scopes that are too broad (a security risk) or the wrong scopes (it will fail), so you verify them against least-privilege needs.

quiz.q: Name two things you must NOT include in a prompt when asking an AI to generate a script.
quiz.answer: Secrets such as client secrets or passwords, and real user or customer PII or tenant identifiers.
quiz.why: Public LLMs may log or train on input, so credentials and PII must never be pasted into a prompt; use placeholders instead.

quiz.q: In one sentence, give a good prompt pattern for generating a PowerShell script with AI.
quiz.answer: State the goal, the environment and modules, the constraints and error handling, and require -WhatIf and comments explaining each step.
quiz.why: A precise prompt that specifies goal, environment, constraints, safety, and explanation produces safer, more accurate, and reviewable code.

body_markdown:
## Why AI is great at PowerShell (and where it bites)

PowerShell is the automation language of endpoint management, and AI is a genuinely strong pair-programmer for it. It can draft a **Microsoft Graph PowerShell SDK** query, scaffold a bulk device operation, write an Intune **remediation script pair**, or explain a script you inherited line by line. The catch: AI also **hallucinates cmdlet and parameter names**, invents Graph scopes, and will happily write destructive code with a straight face. Treated as a fast first draft you fully verify, it is a superpower. Treated as an oracle, it is a production incident waiting to happen.

## Prompt patterns that produce good scripts

Vague prompts produce vague, risky code. State the **goal**, the **environment and modules**, the **constraints**, and the **error handling** you expect.

```text
Write a PowerShell script using the Microsoft Graph PowerShell SDK
to list all Intune-managed Windows devices that haven't checked in
for 30+ days. Requirements: use Connect-MgGraph with least-privilege
scopes, add error handling, include -WhatIf-safe read-only calls,
comment every step, and tell me exactly which Graph scopes are
needed. Do not include any secrets; use placeholders.
```

Asking it to *name the required scopes* and *comment every step* turns the output into something you can actually review.

## A sample generated snippet

Here is the kind of read-only output you might get — and must still read carefully:

```powershell
# Requires: Microsoft.Graph module
# Scopes needed: DeviceManagementManagedDevices.Read.All
Connect-MgGraph -Scopes "DeviceManagementManagedDevices.Read.All"

$cutoff = (Get-Date).AddDays(-30)
Get-MgDeviceManagementManagedDevice -All |
  Where-Object { $_.LastSyncDateTime -lt $cutoff } |
  Select-Object DeviceName, UserPrincipalName, LastSyncDateTime |
  Sort-Object LastSyncDateTime
```

Before trusting it: does `Get-MgDeviceManagementManagedDevice` actually exist with those parameters? Is the property name `LastSyncDateTime` correct? Check the docs — do not assume.

## Remediation script pairs

Intune **remediations** use a **detection** script (exit 1 if the issue is present) plus a **remediation** script (the fix). AI is great for scaffolding both, but a remediation runs on real machines, so safety matters double.

```text
Generate an Intune remediation pair in PowerShell: detection checks
if a registry value HKLM:\...\Foo equals 1; remediation sets it to 1.
Follow Intune exit-code conventions, add error handling, log to a
file, and make the remediation idempotent. Comment every line.
```

## Verify before you run — non-negotiable

This is the most important section of the lesson. **Never run AI-generated scripts in production untested.** The rules:

- **Read every line** and understand what it does. If you can't explain it, you can't run it.
- **Check cmdlet and parameter names** against official docs — AI invents plausible-looking ones.
- **Run `-WhatIf` first** and add confirmation prompts on any destructive cmdlet (`Remove-*`, `Set-*`, `Disable-*`).
- **Test on one pilot device or a tiny pilot group**, never the whole fleet.
- **Verify Graph permission scopes** — least privilege, not the broadest scope the AI grabbed.
- **Review for destructive operations** hidden in the middle of innocent-looking code.
- **Keep secrets and PII out of prompts** — use placeholders for tenant IDs, UPNs, and never paste client secrets.
- **Version-control and peer-review** every script before it goes near production.

## Your task

Use an AI assistant to generate one read-only Microsoft Graph PowerShell script (for example: list devices not checked in for 30 days). Then audit it: confirm every cmdlet and parameter exists in the official docs, identify the Graph scopes it needs, and write two sentences on anything the AI got wrong or that you had to change before you would run it.

slides.title: A sample generated snippet
bullets: Read-only Graph query for stale devices.
Declares the module and scopes up top.
Filters by last sync date.
You must still verify every cmdlet and property.
slides.code:
# Scopes: DeviceManagementManagedDevices.Read.All
Connect-MgGraph -Scopes "DeviceManagementManagedDevices.Read.All"
$cutoff = (Get-Date).AddDays(-30)
Get-MgDeviceManagementManagedDevice -All |
  Where-Object { $_.LastSyncDateTime -lt $cutoff } |
  Select-Object DeviceName, UserPrincipalName, LastSyncDateTime
slides.narration: Here's the kind of read-only snippet you might get back. It declares the scope, connects to Graph, sets a thirty-day cutoff, and filters stale devices. Looks clean, right? But before you trust it, ask: does Get-Mg-Device-Management-Managed-Device actually exist with those parameters? Is the property really called LastSyncDateTime? You check the docs, you don't assume. That habit is what separates safe automation from a broken script.

slides.title: Remediation script pairs
bullets: Detection script: exit 1 if the issue is present.
Remediation script: applies the fix.
AI scaffolds both quickly.
These run on real machines, so safety matters double.
slides.code:
Generate an Intune remediation pair: detection checks if a registry
value equals 1; remediation sets it to 1. Follow Intune exit-code
conventions, add error handling, log to a file, make the remediation
idempotent, and comment every line.
slides.narration: Intune remediations come as a pair: a detection script that exits one if the problem exists, and a remediation script that fixes it. AI is great at scaffolding both. But remember, these run automatically across real machines, so safety matters double. Notice this prompt asks for Intune's exit-code conventions, error handling, logging, and idempotency, meaning it's safe to run twice. Get those right in the prompt and your draft is far closer to production-ready.

slides.title: Verify before you run, part 1
bullets: Never run AI scripts in production untested.
Read every line; if you can't explain it, don't run it.
Check every cmdlet and parameter against official docs.
Run -WhatIf first; guard destructive cmdlets with confirmation.
slides.code:
Get-MgDeviceManagementManagedDevice -All -WhatIf
# Always -WhatIf destructive Remove-* / Set-* / Disable-* first
slides.narration: This is the most important part of the whole lesson, so I'm giving it two slides. Never run AI-generated scripts in production untested. Read every single line, and if you can't explain what it does, you do not run it. Check every cmdlet and parameter against the official docs, because AI invents plausible-looking ones. And run dash-WhatIf first, especially on anything that removes, sets, or disables. WhatIf shows you what would happen without doing it. Use it religiously.

slides.title: Verify before you run, part 2
bullets: Test on one pilot device or a tiny group, never the fleet.
Verify Graph scopes: least privilege, not the broadest grab.
Hunt for destructive operations hidden in innocent code.
Keep secrets and PII out of prompts; version-control and peer-review.
slides.narration: Part two. Test on one pilot device or a tiny pilot group, never the whole fleet, no matter how confident you feel. Verify the Graph scopes the script asks for, and trim them to least privilege rather than the broadest scope the AI grabbed. Read carefully for destructive operations buried in otherwise innocent-looking code. Keep secrets and real user data out of your prompts, use placeholders. And finally, version-control and peer-review every script before it goes anywhere near production. These rules are not optional.

slides.title: Keep secrets and PII out
bullets: Public LLMs may log or train on what you paste.
Never paste client secrets, passwords, or tokens.
Use placeholders for tenant IDs and user UPNs.
Treat the prompt like a public forum post.
slides.narration: One more emphasis on data privacy, because it's easy to slip up. Public LLMs may log your input or train on it. So never, ever paste a client secret, a password, an access token, or real customer data into a prompt. Use placeholders, your-tenant-id, user-at-domain, and swap in the real values locally afterward. A simple mental model: treat every prompt as if you were posting it on a public forum. If you wouldn't post it publicly, don't paste it into the model.
